extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations; instructors and scholars studying PR history and practice
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes four canonical models of public relations (press agentry/publicity, public information, two-way asymmetric, two-way symmetric) and historic/practical campaign techniques used to shape public opinion. Useful for designing, evaluating, or teaching PR campaigns and communication strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press Agentry / Publicity model
rubrics_metrics.description: Purpose: propaganda. Nature of communication: one-way; complete truth not essential. Nature of research: little (often informal 'count the house'). Leading historical figure: P. T. Barnum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners spread the faith of the organization often through incomplete, distorted, or half-true information. Tactics include stunts and media spectacle designed to gain attention; measurement is informal (attendance, media pickup). Appropriate where publicity and attention are primary goals but not where accuracy or two-way understanding is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Information model
rubrics_metrics.description: Purpose: dissemination of information. Nature of communication: one-way; truth important. Nature of research: minimal; may include readability and readership studies. Leading historical figure: Ivy Lee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PR person functions essentially as a 'journalist in residence' whose job is to report objectively about the organization. Use when the goal is to inform publics rather than persuade; evaluate via readership and comprehension measures rather than attitude change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way Asymmetric model
rubrics_metrics.description: Purpose: scientific persuasion. Nature of communication: two-way but imbalanced (effects favor the organization). Nature of research: formative and evaluative research used to identify what publics will accept and to measure campaign effects. Leading historical figure: Edward L. Bernays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners use social science theory and research about attitudes and behavior to plan messages that maximize desired change in publics; feedback is treated as a control mechanism (like a thermostat) to manipulate behavior. Organization aims to change publics, not necessarily itself. Use when targeted persuasion backed by measurement is the objective; avoid conflating feedback with genuine dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way Symmetric model
rubrics_metrics.description: Purpose: mutual understanding between organization and publics. Nature of communication: two-way; balanced effects. Nature of research: formative and evaluative research used to learn perceptions and to counsel management on policy change. Leading practitioners: Bernays (influence), educators, professional leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners act as mediators facilitating dialogue so both management and publics may change. Uses communication theories and research to foster understanding; success measured by improved mutual understanding rather than one-sided attitude change. Appropriate for relationship-building, conflict resolution, and ethical practice; often requires management willingness to adjust policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative research
rubrics_metrics.description: Research used to plan an activity and to choose objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In two-way asymmetric practice, formative research finds what the public will accept and tolerate so messages can be tailored for persuasion. In two-way symmetric practice, formative research identifies how publics perceive the organization and what management might change to better serve public interests; it informs counseling and objective setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative research
rubrics_metrics.description: Research used to determine whether objectives have been met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In asymmetric models, evaluative research measures changes in attitudes and behaviors before and after campaigns to assess campaign effect. In symmetric models, evaluative research measures whether understanding between management and publics has improved. Use pre/post measures, attitude/behavior metrics, and comprehension metrics as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activist organization (campaign structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a formal, organized activist group to sustain and coordinate public relations efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small activist group can win a public relations campaign even as a minority provided it is well organized (e.g., Sons of Liberty, Committees of Correspondence). Formal organization helps maintain sustained activity, coordinate tactics, and project credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of many media (multichannel communication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ a combination of communication tools and media to reach and mobilize publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective campaigns use newspapers, pamphlets, sermons, meetings, broadsides, plays, songs, cartoons, and other media as appropriate. Multichannel approaches increase reach and reinforce messages across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols and slogans
rubrics_metrics.description: Use memorable symbols and concise slogans to compress complex issues and evoke emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbols (e.g., Liberty Tree) and slogans (e.g., 'Taxation without representation') are easily remembered and arouse emotion; they simplify complex ideas into digestible, repeatable units. Use to crystallize public opinion but beware oversimplification and distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-event (staged news events)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create events that would not have occurred except to gain news coverage and shape public perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design staged actions (e.g., Boston Tea Party) to crystallize issues and attract media attention. Pseudo-events can be powerful but risk being seen as manipulative or inauthentic; balance spectacle with credibility when long-term trust matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orchestrating conflict (issue framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shape the interpretation of events and get your side of the story to the public first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public attitudes are influenced by how events are interpreted; practitioners should provide frames that favor their perspective and seek to have that interpretation circulate first. Example: promoting the 'Boston massacre' narrative. Ethically, be mindful of accuracy and consequences of framing conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained saturation campaign
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term, continuous campaign using all available media to move apathetic publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apathetic or indifferent publics often require prolonged exposure across many channels (e.g., the 20-year revolutionary campaign) to change attitudes. Plan for repeated messaging, varied tactics, and endurance rather than expecting rapid, one-off effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner competencies and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential abilities and professional behaviors for PR practitioners: grasping and simplifying complex ideas, strong writing and speaking, tact, reasoned persuasion, and the ability to mediate and compromise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful PR practitioners combine clear thinking and communication skills (examples: Hamilton, Madison, Kendall). Effective styles include tactfulness, avoiding ad hominem attacks, reasoning with opponents, crafting messages the target audience will accept, and using compromise where appropriate. Competence also includes knowing when to act as a journalist, a persuader, or a mediator depending on the model employed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication model framing (linear vs. interactive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of communication model affects strategy: linear Source→Message→Medium→Receiver models presuppose one-way influence; interactive/symmetric models treat parties as peers in dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linear models align with one-way and two-way asymmetric practice where the source controls messages; symmetric practice favors interactive models that avoid fixed 'source'/'receiver' labels and emphasize reciprocal influence. Selecting the model clarifies objectives (inform, persuade, or mutual understanding) and evaluation metrics.
